description: ChangeProof checks flood claims against NASA and ISRO's NISAR radar, which sees through cloud, and gives a plain verdict anyone can understand. Built on the January 2026 floods in southern Mozambique for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. Skills: Python, machine learning, Next.js, React and cloud deployment.
summary: ChangeProof is an interactive web app that checks flood claims against radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission. After a flood, claims spread fast: "the town is underwater", "that village is fine". Optical satellite images are often useless because floods come with cloud, and flood maps mean little to most people. ChangeProof uses NISAR's L-band radar, which sees through cloud, to detect new open water by comparing passes before and during a flood. A user types a claim in plain plain words, and ChangeProof gives a plain verdict (Supported, Not supported, Not provable, Contradicted or Not observable), the evidence behind it, and the exact time of the satellite pass. We built it on the January 2026 floods in southern Mozambique, using the NISAR pass of 17 January 2026, and checked our water detection against Copernicus emergency flood maps. It is honest by design: when radar cannot settle a claim, it says so.
details:
What it does

ChangeProof turns satellite radar into plain answers. A user types a flood claim, such as "Chókwè was flooded on 17 January", and gets a verdict with the evidence: how much of the area around the place was newly under open water, and when NISAR saw it. Every verdict is stamped "as of 17 Jan 2026, 03:42 UTC" and labelled Beta.

How it works

1. NISAR GCOV radar images (Beta) for three areas of the Limpopo valley are compared: before the flood (5 January 2026) and during it (17 January 2026). Calm open water reflects radar away, so new water appears dark.

2. A LightGBM model, trained on one area and tested once on another it never saw, marks new open water. On the held-out area it agrees with the Copernicus flood map at IoU 0.57.

3. A language model only reads the claim into place, date and type, with a rule-based parser as backup. Fixed rules on measured numbers decide the verdict: 10% or more new water within 3 km counts as flooded. Damage claims are always "Not provable", because radar sees water, not damage.

4. The website shows a 3D globe with NASA's real cloud image of 17 January, a radar sweep that reveals the flood, and a detailed before/after map with the Copernicus outline for comparison.

Benefits and intended impact

Aid coordinators can check reports before sending help, fact-checkers can test viral flood claims, and flood insurance schemes can confirm flooding at a place. Forecasts warned early in this flood; ChangeProof is the step after: where the water went and which claims are true.

Honesty and limits

Radar cannot prove water is absent under trees, crops or buildings, so ChangeProof never turns silence into "false". We say "agreement with Copernicus", never accuracy. It is one event and three areas, on Beta data with one flood-time pass. We tested a flooded-vegetation layer, set the pass mark in advance, and dropped it when it failed.

Tools

Python and LightGBM for radar processing; Next.js, React and TypeScript for the web app; MapLibre GL and GSAP for the globe; Leaflet for the detailed map; Node.js on Vercel; Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite via OpenRouter for reading claims. Code: https://github.com/AqeelDEV/changeproof

What's next

NISAR's validated data (from October 2026) and a second flood as an independent test; combining NISAR with Sentinel-1 for a look every two to three days; new detectors for other flood types.
